metadata.name: Hypertension (essential/primary)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine (chronic) — but hypertensive emergency (>180/120 with target-organ damage) is a medical emergency
metadata.severity: Grade 1 (140-159/90-99), Grade 2 (160-179/100-109), Grade 3 (>=180/110) per ESC/ESH; asymptomatic yet high lifetime cardiovascular risk

overview.short_description: Persistently elevated arterial blood pressure (office BP >=140/90 mmHg, or >=130/80 by ACC/AHA), usually asymptomatic, a leading modifiable risk factor for stroke, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.
overview.detailed_description: Hypertension is a chronic condition defined by sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure. In >90% of adults it is 'essential/primary' (no single identifiable cause); the remainder is 'secondary' to a definable cause (renal, endocrine, drug-induced, etc.). Diagnosis requires elevated readings confirmed on repeat measurement, ideally with out-of-office measurement (ambulatory or home BP) to exclude white-coat effect. Because it is usually silent, it is detected by screening and its importance lies in long-term cardiovascular and renal risk rather than acute symptoms.
overview.pathophysiology: Blood pressure = cardiac output x systemic vascular resistance. Essential hypertension reflects a combination of increased vascular resistance (arteriolar remodelling, endothelial dysfunction, reduced nitric-oxide bioavailability), inappropriate renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation, sympathetic overactivity, and renal sodium handling that resets pressure-natriuresis to a higher set point. Chronic elevation causes arterial stiffening, left-ventricular hypertrophy, and end-organ damage.
overview.etiology: Primary (essential): polygenic predisposition plus environment (high sodium/low potassium diet, obesity, inactivity, excess alcohol, ageing arterial stiffening). Secondary causes to consider especially if young, resistant, or abrupt onset: chronic kidney disease, renovascular disease, primary aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, thyroid/parathyroid disease, obstructive sleep apnoea, coarctation, and drugs (NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, sympathomimetics/decongestants, ciclosporin, liquorice, cocaine/amphetamines).
overview.natural_history: Typically develops gradually from middle age; without treatment, sustained elevation accelerates atherosclerosis and produces target-organ damage over years to decades (LVH, heart failure, stroke, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease).
overview.prognosis: Excellent when detected early and controlled; each ~10 mmHg reduction in systolic BP substantially lowers stroke and coronary risk. Prognosis worsens with grade, duration, coexisting diabetes/CKD, and established target-organ damage.

prevalence.value: ~30-45% of adults worldwide; rises with age (>60% over age 60). Global estimate ~1.3 billion adults (WHO).

incidence.value: High lifetime incidence; most adults develop hypertension by old age in high-sodium populations.

mortality.value: Leading global contributor to cardiovascular death; attributable to millions of deaths/year via stroke and ischaemic heart disease (WHO).

epidemiology.age_groups: Prevalence increases steadily with age; isolated systolic hypertension predominates in the elderly.
epidemiology.sex_predominance: Slightly higher in men before ~55; women catch up and exceed after menopause.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; rising burden in low- and middle-income countries (including North Africa/MENA) with dietary transition and under-treatment.
epidemiology.seasonal_pattern: BP tends to be modestly higher in cold weather.

risk_factors.lifestyle: High dietary sodium, low potassium (low fruit/vegetable intake), physical inactivity, psychosocial stress, poor sleep.
risk_factors.smoking: Causes acute BP rises and accelerates atherosclerosis; major additive cardiovascular risk (though chronic smoking's effect on baseline BP is modest).
risk_factors.alcohol: Excess intake raises BP dose-dependently; reduction lowers BP.
risk_factors.obesity: Strong dose-dependent risk factor; central adiposity especially. Weight loss is one of the most effective non-drug interventions.
risk_factors.diabetes: Frequently coexists (metabolic syndrome); together sharply increase cardiovascular and renal risk.
risk_factors.pregnancy: Pre-existing (chronic) hypertension and pregnancy-related hypertension/pre-eclampsia are distinct entities requiring specific management.
risk_factors.occupation: Shift work, high-strain jobs, noise exposure associated with modestly higher BP.
risk_factors.family_history: Positive family history is a strong risk factor (polygenic heritability).
risk_factors.genetic_factors: Polygenic; rare monogenic forms (e.g., Liddle syndrome, glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism) — consider in young/resistant cases.
risk_factors.medications: NSAIDs, combined oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, sympathomimetic decongestants, ciclosporin/tacrolimus, erythropoietin, VEGF inhibitors, liquorice.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Chronic kidney disease, obstructive sleep apnoea, endocrine disorders (raise secondary-HTN probability).

chief_complaints.importance: Low — nonspecific; usually only with very high BP

symptoms.importance: Defining feature — hypertension is 'silent'; diagnosis is by measurement, not symptoms
Red flag when acute (retinopathy / malignant hypertension)

negative_findings.finding: No headache, visual change, chest pain, or neurological deficit
negative_findings.why_important: Makes hypertensive emergency/urgency far less likely — supports routine chronic management

negative_findings.finding: Normal home/ambulatory BP despite high office readings
negative_findings.why_important: Suggests white-coat hypertension rather than sustained hypertension

history_questions.question: How long has your blood pressure been high, and what have your home readings been?
history_questions.why_ask: Distinguishes new vs long-standing; home data reduces white-coat effect

history_questions.question: Any headache, chest pain, breathlessness, visual change, or weakness/numbness?
history_questions.why_ask: Screens for hypertensive emergency and target-organ damage

history_questions.question: Do you take NSAIDs, decongestants, oral contraceptives, steroids, or use liquorice/stimulants?
Snoring, witnessed apnoea, daytime sleepiness?
history_questions.why_ask: Obstructive sleep apnoea is a common secondary/contributing cause

history_questions.question: Family history of hypertension, stroke, kidney disease, or early heart disease?

physical_examination.examination: Blood pressure — both arms, correct cuff size, seated after rest; repeat and average

physical_examination.expected_finding: May show LVH signs, loud A2
Hypertensive retinopathy (AV nicking, haemorrhages, papilloedema in emergency)

physical_examination.examination: Peripheral pulses / radio-femoral delay; renal/abdominal bruit
physical_examination.expected_finding: Delay suggests coarctation; bruit suggests renovascular disease

vital_signs.heart_rate: Usually normal; tachycardia may suggest phaeochromocytoma/hyperthyroidism/anxiety
vital_signs.blood_pressure: Elevated by definition; >=180/120 with symptoms = emergency
vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: Normal unless complicated by heart failure

laboratory_tests.expected_result: Usually normal; low K+ may suggest primary aldosteronism

laboratory_tests.test_name: TSH; aldosterone:renin ratio; metanephrines; overnight dexamethasone
laboratory_tests.indication: Only if secondary hypertension suspected (young, resistant, hypokalaemia, paroxysms)

imaging.imaging_type: Renal ultrasound / Doppler / CT or MR angiography
imaging.when_needed: Suspected renovascular or renal parenchymal disease
imaging.expected_findings: Renal artery stenosis, asymmetric kidneys, structural disease

ecg.when_needed: At diagnosis for all (baseline) and if cardiac symptoms
ecg.findings: Left ventricular hypertrophy (Sokolow-Lyon/Cornell criteria), strain pattern, prior infarction, LA enlargement, AF.

other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Renal biopsy only in specific parenchymal disease work-up

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Office BP >=140/90 mmHg on repeated visits (ESC/ESH, WHO) or >=130/80 (ACC/AHA 2017). Confirm with ambulatory (ABPM daytime average >=135/85) or home BP monitoring (HBPM >=135/85) to exclude white-coat hypertension.
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: Cardiovascular risk scores (e.g., SCORE2/SCORE2-OP, QRISK, ASCVD pooled cohort) guide treatment thresholds and targets.

cutoff_values.value: Grade 1 140-159/90-99; Grade 2 160-179/100-109; Grade 3 >=180/110; ABPM/HBPM diagnostic threshold 135/85; hypertensive emergency >=180/120 with acute target-organ damage.

differential_diagnosis.disease: Secondary hypertension (renal, aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, OSA, Cushing, coarctation)
differential_diagnosis.differences: Young onset, resistant, hypokalaemia, paroxysms, specific features
Acute target-organ damage present (emergency) vs absent (urgency)
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Chest pain, neuro deficit, dyspnoea, visual loss
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any chest pain, weakness, breathlessness, visual change?

diagnostic_questions.question: What are your averaged home BP readings over a week?
Any spells of sweating, palpitations, and headache together?

next_best_question.question: Can you measure and log your BP at home twice daily for 7 days?
next_best_question.branching_logic: High -> confirm HTN and stage; Normal -> white-coat, reassess risk

next_best_test.why: Confirms diagnosis and excludes white-coat effect before lifelong treatment

next_best_test.test: Baseline bloods (electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, HbA1c, lipids), ACR, ECG
next_best_test.why: Assess target-organ damage and global cardiovascular risk
next_best_test.expected_outcome: Guides treatment threshold and drug choice

red_flags.finding: BP >=180/120 WITH chest pain, breathlessness, neurological deficit, severe headache, or visual loss
red_flags.immediate_action: Treat as hypertensive emergency — same-day emergency assessment; controlled IV BP lowering in hospital

red_flags.finding: New confusion, focal weakness, or slurred speech
Severe headache with visual disturbance and papilloedema
BP high in pregnancy with headache/visual symptoms/epigastric pain

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected secondary hypertension needing specialist tests; resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on 3 drugs incl. a diuretic); accelerated/malignant hypertension without acute complications (same-day specialist).
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Young patients (<40) with hypertension; suspected endocrine cause; specialist advice for complex comorbidity.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Hypertensive emergency (BP >=180/120 with acute target-organ damage), eclampsia/pre-eclampsia, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary oedema.

late: Left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure

initial_management.supportive_care: Confirm diagnosis with out-of-office BP; stage severity; assess total cardiovascular risk and target-organ damage before/with starting treatment.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): ACE inhibitor or ARB; Calcium-channel blocker; Thiazide-like diuretic; Spironolactone. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG136_2026.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Reduce sodium (<5-6 g salt/day), DASH-style diet rich in fruit/vegetables, weight loss if overweight, regular aerobic activity, limit alcohol, stop smoking, reduce caffeine if excessive.
initial_management.follow_up: Review after starting/adjusting therapy (e.g., every 2-4 weeks until controlled), then at least annually with BP, bloods (U&E after ACEi/ARB/diuretic), and risk review; encourage home monitoring.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: First-line per major guidelines: ACE inhibitor or ARB (especially if <55 or diabetic), calcium-channel blocker (especially if >=55 or Black African/Caribbean ancestry), and thiazide-like diuretic; combine stepwise. Add spironolactone for resistant HTN if K+ permits. Beta-blockers for specific indications. Targets individualised (commonly <140/90, tighter e.g. <130/80 in many patients if tolerated).

patient_education.home_advice: High blood pressure is usually silent but important; take medicines every day even when you feel well, check your BP at home, cut down salt, stay active, keep a healthy weight, limit alcohol, and stop smoking.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: ارتفاع ضغط الدم غالباً بلا أعراض لكنه خطير. تناول أدويتك يومياً حتى لو شعرت بخير، وقِس ضغطك في المنزل، وقلّل الملح، وحافظ على النشاط والوزن الصحي، وقلّل الكحول وتوقّف عن التدخين.
patient_education.prevention: Maintain healthy weight, low-salt/high-potassium diet, regular exercise, moderate alcohol, no smoking; periodic BP checks from mid-adulthood.
patient_education.warning_signs: Seek urgent care for severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, sudden weakness/numbness, slurred speech, or visual loss.

prevention.lifestyle: Salt reduction, DASH diet, weight control, exercise, limited alcohol, no smoking — primary prevention and treatment.
prevention.screening: Opportunistic/periodic BP measurement in all adults; more frequent if risk factors.

evidence.evidence_level: High — large randomised trials and meta-analyses (BP lowering reduces stroke/MI/heart failure).
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG136_2026; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong recommendations across ESC/ESH, NICE NG136, ACC/AHA, WHO.

Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): ACE inhibitor or ARB; Calcium-channel blocker; Thiazide-like diuretic; Spironolactone. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed.
